title: Four good questions about the 'factors that affect learning' - and my replies
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Replying to reader responses, Skelton restates his central point that factors such as a curriculum, evidence or resources are not themselves learning, using a broom and cleaning analogy. He explains that a learning lens means a shared definition of learning across the whole school community, and that schools should look for evidence of learning before tinkering with factors. He admits he failed to do this as an acting head, writing a curriculum without checking whether day-to-day learning was happening. He accepts that the factors will never all align perfectly, so leaders should work backwards from the evidence to the factor most obstructing learning. He ends by offering the curriculum checklist as a sample of the diagnostic tools he recommends.
points: Having a curriculum, resources or teaching does not mean learning is happening; they only matter when they are in good condition and used well.
A learning lens requires one shared definition of learning among leaders, teachers, students, governors and parents.
Start with evidence of learning and only then pick the factor most hindering it, as you would check the floor before buying cleaning equipment.
Perfect alignment of all factors is unrealistic, so improvement means prioritising the worst obstacle and leaving others for later.
quotes: A broom is not ‘cleaning’. Cleaning doesn’t happen because we own a broom. Cleaning happens when our broom is in a condition that helps learning happen and, most importantly, when we use it appropriately.

A ‘lens’ is the framework we use to focus and make judgements about what matters. To have a ‘learning lens’ means that we have to have a definition of learning that is shared across the school, one that is shared by school leadership, teachers, children and students, governors and Board members, and parents.

The main reason we start with evidence about learning first rather than the factors that affect learning is that our lens is a learning lens and not a factors lens. It is the quality and quantity of engaged learning - for good or not so good - that will underpin our work on the factors that affect learning and which factors we might choose.

To use our cleaning analogy, if the floor is clean, we don’t need to worry about the factors that affect its cleanliness. If it isn’t clean, we can begin to identify why it isn’t clean, which factors are affecting its cleanliness and which we need to deal with first.

In the real world, though, no. Schools are complex human places. In the actual world we live in there are always going to be one or more factors that are somewhat out of alignment and which might be getting in the way of learning happening.

But for most of us, there has to be a large element of backward planning involved if we are in schools that have been up and running for some time. We have to look at the evidence about the quality and quantity of engaged learning that is happening and, if it is unsatisfactory, identify the factor or factors that are most getting in the way of learning and work on those first.

These checklists aren’t perfect. There will always be something to add or take away to make them fit your particular circumstances. But they are derived from the best practices we saw in hundreds of schools in tens of different countries.
